thread.title: Charting a bearish technical tilt, S&P 500 bounces from 200-day average

author: Michael Ashbaugh
title: Charting a bearish technical tilt, S&P 500 bounces from 200-day average
text:
Editor’s Note: This is a free edition of The Technical Indicator, a daily MarketWatch subscriber newsletter. To get this column each market day, click here.
Broadly speaking, the late-March market downdraft has registered as aggressive, inflicting bigger-picture technical damage.
Against this backdrop, the S&P 500 has maintained major support — an area matching the 200-day moving average — and the quality of its prevailing rally attempt should be a useful bull-bear gauge.
Before detailing the U.S. markets’ wider view, the S&P 500’s SPX, +0.50% hourly chart highlights the past two weeks.
As illustrated, the S&P has nailed its 200-day moving average, and rallied respectably from one-month lows.
Tactically, significant resistance broadly spans from 2,673 to 2,695, the latter matching the 2017 peak. This area also matched Thursday’s session high (2,695), and capped a technically damaging two-day downdraft.
Similarly, the Dow Jones Industrial Average has rallied respectably from the range bottom.
Consider that Monday’s 669-point spike marked its biggest daily point gain since 2008, and the third-largest on record.
Still, technical damage has been inflicted, better illustrated on the daily chart. Near-term resistance matches the early-March low (24,217) and is followed by the bottom of last week’s gap.
Against this backdrop, the Nasdaq Composite has rallied sharply from one-month lows.
Tactically, the 50-day moving average marks an inflection point, currently 7,289, closely matching its trendline, illustrated below.
Widening the view to six months adds perspective.
On this wider view, the Nasdaq has signaled an intermediate-term trend shift, building on the March bearish island reversal.
Specifically, the index has violated its 50-day moving average, and trendline support, while also notching a “lower low” versus the early-March low.
Separately, the 50-day moving average’s slope has ticked lower, also consistent with a trend shift.
Tactically, an inflection point matches the early-March low (7,084) and the Nasdaq’s nearly immediate reversal higher is a modest positive. Still, firmer overhead matches the trendline, and an eventual close higher would more firmly neutralize the March downdraft.
Looking elsewhere, the Dow Jones Industrial Average has plunged from a symmetrical triangle, tagging a four-month closing low.
Though Monday’s 669-point spike marked the Dow’s third-best on record, the bounce was partly a function of the preceding downdraft’s aggressiveness.
Tactically, significant resistance spans from about 24,719 to 24,876, levels matching the 2017 close and 2017 peak. An eventual close higher would stabilize the backdrop.
Meanwhile, the S&P 500’s price action remains technical even amid recent volatility.
To start, the March downdraft has resolved a bearish double top defined by the February and March peaks.
Still, the S&P has thus far maintained its 200-day moving average, currently 2,587, punctuating its second successful retest in as many months. To reiterate, significant resistance matches the 2017 peak (2,695) and the eventual retest is worth tracking.
The bigger picture Collectively, the late-March downdraft has registered as technically aggressive, inflicting damage to the bigger-picture backdrop.
Though the prevailing technicals are not one-size-fits-all, the backdrop generally supports a bearish intermediate-term bias pending repairs.
Moving to the small-caps, the iShares Russell 2000 ETF IWM, +0.05% has violated well-defined support, circa 155.50, and the 50-day moving average.
It’s thus far narrowly maintained next support (150.50) though the rally attempt has initially been fueled by decreased volume. To reiterate, market bears will point to a developing double top, originating from record highs.
Meanwhile, the S&P MidCap 400’s backdrop remains incrementally softer. Still, the MDY has thus far maintained a posture atop the 200-day moving average, currently 332.90.
More broadly, the small- and mid-cap benchmarks have whipsawed since violating trendline support eight weeks ago.
Against this backdrop, the SPDR Trust S&P 500 has violated major support matching the 2017 peak.
Though the SPY has maintained the 200-day moving average, its initial rally attempt has been fueled by decreased volume.
Tactically, resistance spans from 268.60 to 268.90 — the former matching the 2017 peak — and a close higher would mark a step toward stabilization.
Summing up the backdrop All told, the March downdraft has inflicted damage, contributing to a bearish intermediate-term technical tilt.
Against this backdrop, the S&P 500 has thus far maintained major support, detailed previously.
Recall three inflection points:
The 200-day moving average, currently 2,587. The S&P’s 10% correction mark of 2,586. The March closing low of 2,581. To reiterate, last week’s low (2,585.9) and the weekly close (2,588.3) effectively matched support.
The question now is the quality of the S&P 500’s rally attempt, currently underway.
When gauging the quality, an inflection point spans from 2,641 to 2,647, and the S&P has already closed higher.
On further strength, more important overhead matches the S&P’s breakdown point, spanning from 2,673 to 2,695. To reiterate, a swift reversal higher would place the brakes on bearish momentum.
Beyond intermediate-term issues, the S&P 500’s primary uptrend is intact to the extent it continues to find support near the 200-day moving average.
See also: Charting technical cross currents, market bears resurface ahead of the Fed.
Tuesday’s Watch List The charts below detail names that are technically well positioned. These are radar screen names — sectors or stocks poised to move in the near term. For the original comments on the stocks below, see The Technical Indicator Library.
Drilling down further, the SPDR Gold Trust GLD, -0.62% has come to life amid recent market volatility.
As illustrated, the shares have rallied from the range bottom, rising to challenge well-defined resistance matching the September peak.
More broadly, the prevailing range top matches major overhead — spanning from about 128.30 to 129.50 — illustrated on the five-year chart.
Tactically, the current upturn marks the third recent retest, and major resistance is frequently cleared on the third or fourth independent test. An eventual breakout opens the path to less-charted territory, and potentially material follow-through.
Similarly, the United States Oil Fund USO, -0.15% profiled last week, is acting well technically. The fund tracks the price of West Texas Intermediate (WTI) light, sweet crude oil.
As illustrated, the shares have knifed from a symmetrical triangle, rising to challenge two-year highs.
The January peak (13.30) marks the USO’s best level since November 2015, and it remains under siege to conclude the first quarter.
Conversely, the trendline closely matches major support, the 2016 peak of 12.45, illustrated on the four-year chart. A sustained posture higher supports a firmly bullish bias.
Charting the U.S. sub-sector backdrop Moving to specific sectors, the U.S. sub-sector backdrop continues to soften. Quickly consider three vulnerable groups as well as two pockets of relative strength.
To start, the SPDR S&P Homebuilders ETF XHB, +0.17% remains tenuously positioned.
Technically, the group has established a bearish descending triangle, challenging support broadly spanning from about 39.50 to 41.00. An eventual violation opens the path to potentially material downside follow-through.
Conversely, a close atop trendline resistance, circa 42, would neutralize the bearish pattern.
Meanwhile, the Materials Select Sector SPDR XLB, +0.89% — profiled last week — has violated major support amid increased volume.
The downturn builds on the group’s double top, the “M” formation defined by the February and March peaks.
Tactically, the 200-day moving average, currently 57.90, pivots to resistance. The group’s backdrop supports a bearish bias pending a close higher.
Similarly, the Health Care Select Sector SPDR XLV, +0.64% has violated its 200-day moving average, pressured amid increased volume.
Here again, the downturn resolves a double top defined by the February and March peaks. An eventual close atop the 200-day, currently 82.40, would mark a step toward stabilization.
Pockets of sector strength persist Conversely, pockets of sector resilience persist. Two groups stand out:
To start, the VanEck Vectors Semiconductor ETF SMH, -0.14% is acting well technically. The group has staged an orderly pullback from record territory, maintaining a posture atop the 50-day moving average.
Meanwhile, the SPDR S&P Biotech ETF XBI, -1.11% is also acting relatively well.
As illustrated, the group has maintained its breakout point (88.50) punctuating an orderly pullback from record highs. Also consider that the initial rally from support was fueled by increased volume.
Collectively, pockets of sector strength persist, though leadership is increasingly fading, a near- to intermediate-term market headwind.
